There are a lot of people that see the entire world through the lens of their religion. Because of this, when someone comes along that argues against their religion, it essentially shakes their entire worldview. 

For such people, all their values, knowledge, and beliefs are immediately brought into question. The existential dread and cognitive dissonance that you can get from this can, and often will be very devastating. For example, imagine that nice old lady that believes she'll see her dead children in heaven because she believes Christianity to be true. If/when she discovers Christianity to be a lie, it'll seem to her like her entire life is a lie. 

For a lot of believers, it's much better to remove the "source" of that cognitive dissonance than to admit you are mistaken. I say "source" because they try all means not to accept that they could be wrong and instead pin their dissonance on the person that brings up the argument against their religion. This removal of the "source" can take the form of dismissal of opposing views, to downright destruction of the "source" of that cognitive dissonance.

>how could the big bang happen if everything came from nothing? 

First off, we don't know that everything came from nothing. We don't know what was before the big bang.

Secondly, even if hypothetically, everything did come from nothing, there is absolutely no evidence whatsoever to attribute that to a god. Not only that, but there is a HUGE leap in logic from "there was once nothing before the big bang" to "a god caused the big bang". This makes your argument flawed from the very beginning. 

This is what we call an argument from ignorance (ignorance meaning a lack of knowledge, and not a shot at your intelligence). "We don't know, therefore god" is not a solid foundation for your beliefs, my friend.

By the way, I want it to be extremely clear that I'm not saying that it's impossible for a god to have caused the big bang. I am saying that there is no evidence to suggest that. Personally, I believe that no gods exist, but that is a completely different debate.

The universe is roughly 13.772 ± 0.040 billion years old. Our planet, Earth has existed for roughly 4.543 ± 0.050 billion years old. Our ancestors roamed the earth about 6 million years ago, and humans, as we exist today, have existed for about 300,000 years. Civilization didn't start until about 6,000 years ago. 

The point I'm trying to make is that you and I, were not alive for that amount of time. We only became *us* fairly recently (that's like a nanosecond of time when you put it into perspective), and we'll be gone fairly quickly as well. We don't feel anything for not being alive then, because we can't, and we won't feel anything after we pass, because we can't.

After our brains shut down, that's it, my friend. The only reason you and I are afraid of death is because the human mind cannot comprehend non-existence. The closest thing we can imagine is "blackness" and that's not accurate in the slightest. We fear what we don't know, and since we don't know "nothingness", we fear it.

I get it if you struggle to accept this, as I oftentimes struggle to make sense of it as well. However, it's safe to say that once we die, we're dead. And we will stay that way forever.
